clinicalPearls: Rare autosomal recessive disorder of the free hydroxyproline degradation pathway caused by deficiency of hydroxyproline oxidase (4-hydroxyproline dehydrogenase), encoded by PRODH2.
Biochemical hallmark is a marked isolated increase in plasma free hydroxyproline, with a corresponding rise in urinary free (not peptide-bound) hydroxyproline.

Considered a benign metabolic variant; the neurological and intellectual problems described in the earliest case reports are now generally attributed to ascertainment bias rather than to the enzyme defect.
Free hydroxyproline arises largely from the turnover of collagen-derived hydroxyproline; the block prevents its conversion to 4-hydroxy-glutamate semialdehyde and onward metabolism.
Crucially distinct from disorders of proline metabolism: the enzyme is specific for hydroxyproline and does not affect proline, so proline levels are normal.
Must be differentiated from raised total urinary hydroxyproline seen in high-bone-turnover states, where the hydroxyproline is peptide-bound and derived from collagen breakdown.
No dietary restriction or specific therapy is indicated; recognition mainly prevents unnecessary further investigation.
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating the selective free-hydroxyproline elevation with normal proline, ideally supported by PRODH2 analysis.
reference.pathophysiology: Hydroxyprolinaemia is caused by deficient activity of hydroxyproline oxidase (also termed 4-hydroxyproline dehydrogenase), a mitochondrial flavoenzyme encoded by PRODH2 that catalyses the first step in the catabolism of free trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline, oxidising it to delta-1-pyrroline-3-hydroxy-5-carboxylate. Free hydroxyproline is generated during the physiological turnover of collagen and other hydroxyproline-containing proteins, since hydroxyproline is formed post-translationally by prolyl hydroxylation and cannot be reincorporated into protein once liberated. Loss of the oxidase blocks this degradative route, so free hydroxyproline accumulates in plasma and is excreted in urine in its free form. The enzyme is distinct from proline oxidase (PRODH1), which acts on proline; consequently the defect is specific to hydroxyproline handling and does not perturb proline catabolism or the interconnected glutamate and ornithine pathways. Because no neurotoxic intermediates accumulate, the biochemical lesion appears to be clinically silent in most reported individuals.
additionalDifferentials: Hyperprolinaemia type 1 (proline oxidase/PRODH1 deficiency, affecting proline rather than hydroxyproline)
Prolidase deficiency (impaired recycling of proline and hydroxyproline from dipeptides)
Raised total urinary hydroxyproline from high bone turnover (Paget disease, hyperparathyroidism, growth)
Iminoglycinuria (renal transport defect affecting proline, hydroxyproline and glycine)
Coincidental elevation from collagen-related connective tissue disease or fracture healing
Other benign incidental aminoacidurias detected on screening
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative plasma amino acids showing isolated elevation of free hydroxyproline with normal proline
Urine amino acid analysis confirming increased free (non-peptide-bound) hydroxyproline
Fractionation of urinary hydroxyproline into free versus peptide-bound to exclude collagen-turnover causes
Markers of bone turnover and calcium metabolism to exclude high-turnover states
PRODH2 gene analysis to confirm the diagnosis
Family biochemical screening of siblings given autosomal recessive inheritance
redFlags: Predominantly peptide-bound urinary hydroxyproline suggests a bone or collagen-turnover disorder rather than the primary enzyme defect
Concurrent elevation of proline points instead to a hyperprolinaemia subtype or prolidase deficiency
Significant neurological or developmental abnormality should prompt search for an independent cause
Skin ulceration or recurrent infection suggests prolidase deficiency rather than hydroxyprolinaemia
reference.prognosis: Hydroxyprolinaemia is considered a benign biochemical trait compatible with normal health and life expectancy, and no morbidity has been reliably attributed to the isolated elevation of free hydroxyproline. Its recognition is chiefly of value in avoiding unwarranted investigation and reassuring affected families.
pitfalls: Mistaking a benign free-hydroxyproline elevation for evidence of a serious metabolic or bone disorder
Failing to fractionate urinary hydroxyproline, thereby confusing collagen-turnover elevation with the primary defect
Confusing hydroxyprolinaemia with the clinically important hyperprolinaemias because of the similar names
Attributing incidental developmental problems to the metabolic finding without further evaluation
Overlooking prolidase deficiency, which also raises hydroxyproline-containing dipeptides but has a distinct phenotype
references: Standard inborn errors of metabolism textbooks
management: No disease-specific therapy is required, as hydroxyprolinaemia is a benign biochemical trait compatible with normal health
Reassurance of affected individuals and families, avoiding unnecessary investigation or treatment prompted by the incidental biochemical finding
Confirmation of the diagnosis by demonstrating isolated elevation of free hydroxyproline with normal proline and, where available, PRODH2 gene analysis
Differentiation from high-bone-turnover states, in which raised urinary hydroxyproline is peptide-bound and collagen-derived
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance with biochemical screening of siblings
